title: Blip 02 — Dialogue Voices, a Second Cast
short: 104 dialogue blips: 13 new speakers, 13 synthesis methods, none of them a Blip 01 voice. Same cues, same names.
body:
104 dialogue sounds. 13 new speakers, each a different synthesis method.

A second cast for text advance dialogue, the ticks and chirps a text box plays as a line types out. It works on its own, and it is built to sit beside Blip 01, Dialogue Voices for Text Advance without ever sounding like it: same 8 cues, same file names, 13 new voices.

Licence, up front

Royalty free. Commercial use. No credit required. No revenue limit, no unit cap, no second licence to buy later if your game does well. Use it in as many projects as you like, on any platform. The one thing you may not do is resell the sounds themselves as sounds. The full plain language terms ship as LICENSE.txt, with a copy paste credit line if you want one.

Everything is synthesised from code. No recordings, no sample libraries, no third party clips, so there is no upstream licence behind this one and nobody can content ID claim these sounds against your project.

Hear it first

There is a free demo on this page with four complete voices, chosen by measurement from the darkest to the brightest end of the cast, all 8 cues each, copied unaltered. Play their four blips back to back before you pay.

The new cast

  • Giant. Huge and unhurried. A low tone with its own octave under it, swelling in rather than striking. 151 Hz
  • Captain. Gravel and command. A folded tone, rough at the top and kept low. 311 Hz
  • Diver. Heard through water: muffled, with a fast wobble in the pitch. 376 Hz
  • Sage. Old and wise. A soft reed with a slow tremble in the pitch. 811 Hz
  • Envoy. From somewhere far away. Partials like a bell's, which do not line up as a chord. 1013 Hz
  • Jester. A rubber face. The vowel slides from oh to ee inside every glyph. 1164 Hz
  • Bard. A plucked string for a voice. Every glyph is a little note. 1272 Hz
  • Comm Link. A voice over a radio: a narrow band, a little overdriven, with a squelch tail. 1398 Hz
  • Imp. Quick and mischievous. Each glyph drops in pitch like a flicked rubber band. 2255 Hz
  • Hologram. A projected interface. Glassy FM tones that settle as they fade. 2601 Hz
  • Android. Synthetic but articulate. A synced resonance sweeping like a formant. 3418 Hz
  • Familiar. A small companion animal that answers in two quick rising chirps. 4682 Hz
  • Fae. Tiny and glittering. Two tones ring modulated together, gone almost at once. 5741 Hz

A Karplus Strong string, two operator FM, a ring modulator, a wavefolder, windowed oscillator sync, two moving formants, a telephone band with a squelch tail, inharmonic partials, a falling chirp. The figures are the mean brightness of each voice's own per glyph tick, measured off the shipped WAV files.

Two packs, 26 voices, no collisions

Inside this pack all 78 pairs of voices are separated by at least 12 percent in brightness or 25 percent in length. Across the series the same check runs over both casts together: 26 voices, 325 pairs, 169 of them a new voice against a Blip 01 voice, and 325 of 325 are separated. The check is proven to fire, too: each Blip 01 voice planted back in as a copy pitched 3 percent away was caught, 13 of 13. The result ships as series_proof.json.

Every speaker ships the same 8 cues as Blip 01

  • blip_01. tick for one glyph, take 1
  • blip_02. tick for one glyph, take 2
  • blip_03. tick for one glyph, take 3
  • soft. the same voice lowered, for asides and whispers
  • loud. the same voice raised, for shouting and emphasis
  • question. rising inflection, for a line ending in ?
  • exclaim. emphatic hit, for a line ending in !
  • advance. page turn / next line, in this voice

File names are voice then cue, exactly as in Blip 01, so a dialogue system already wired for Blip 01 takes these voices by changing the speaker id and nothing else.

Fit

  • WAV and OGG for every file, 16 bit, 44.1 kHz, mono.
  • One loudness band. The inner 80 percent sits inside 0.85 dB, so switching speaker never changes how loud the text box is.
  • Slow speakers by design. The giant, the sage and a few others tick for 100 ms or more; fire them every second or third glyph, or once per word.
  • 13 declared variation sets, three takes per voice, so a repeated tick never repeats a file.
  • Nothing loops, and no file carries loop points.
  • pack_proof.json ships with the pack: 945 checks, 0 failed.

Honest limits

These are synthesised character voices in the blip tradition, not recorded speech and not a vocal synthesiser. They say that someone is talking; they do not say words. The measurements above are SIGNAL measurements, not a claim that it sounds good. That is what the free demo is for.

AI disclosure, stated truthfully: the code that generates these sounds was written with AI assistance. The sounds themselves are self contained procedural synthesis, oscillators, filters and delay lines evaluated in code, with no generative audio model at any point. The cover art and store graphics are AI generated.
